title: Web Hosting
summary: Learn where websites and apps actually live: shared, VPS, dedicated, cloud and serverless hosting, free static hosts, backends, databases, CDNs, backups and how to pick a host without surprise bills.

lessons.title: What web hosting is
lessons.summary: Learn what a host provides and what happens when someone visits your site.

slides.title: A computer that never sleeps
slides.text:
**Web hosting** = renting space and power on a computer that is:
- always on
- connected to fast internet
- reachable by a public IP

That computer is a **server**.
slides.narration: Web hosting means renting space on a computer that is always switched on, has a fast connection, and can be reached from anywhere on the internet. That computer is called a server, and it lives in a data center.

slides.title: What happens on a visit
slides.text:
1. Browser looks up the domain in **DNS** -> IP
2. Connects to the server (HTTPS, port 443)
3. Server sends files or runs code
4. Browser renders the page
slides.narration: When someone visits your site, their browser first asks DNS for the server's address. Then it opens a secure connection to that server. The server sends back files, or runs your code to build a response, and the browser displays the page.

slides.title: What a host gives you
slides.text:
- **Compute**: CPU and RAM to run code
- **Storage**: disk for files and databases
- **Bandwidth**: data sent to visitors
- **Network**: IP addresses, firewalls
- Often: HTTPS, backups, a dashboard, support
slides.narration: A host provides compute power to run your code, storage for files and data, bandwidth to send pages to visitors, and networking. Many hosts also include extras such as free HTTPS certificates, backups and a friendly dashboard.

slides.title: Domain vs hosting
slides.text:
- **Domain** = the name (`example.com`), bought at a registrar
- **Hosting** = where the site lives
- DNS connects the two

They can be from different companies.
slides.narration: Beginners often mix up domains and hosting. The domain is just the name, bought from a registrar. Hosting is where the website actually lives. DNS records connect the two, and they can come from completely different companies.

slides.title: The main types
slides.text:
From most managed to most control:

**Static hosting -> Serverless -> PaaS -> Shared -> VPS -> Dedicated**

More control = more responsibility.
slides.narration: There are many kinds of hosting. At one end, static hosts and serverless platforms manage almost everything for you. At the other end, virtual private servers and dedicated machines give you full control, along with full responsibility for security and updates.

lessons.notes:
## Definition

**Web hosting** is a service that runs your website or app on servers connected to the internet. Instead of keeping your own computer online 24/7, you rent capacity in a **data center** with redundant power, cooling and network links.

## The request journey

1. The visitor types `example.com`.
2. **DNS** returns the server's IP address.
3. The browser opens a TLS (HTTPS) connection to that IP on port 443.
4. A **web server** (Nginx, Apache, Caddy) or platform receives the request.
5. It returns static files, or passes the request to your **application** (Node, Python, PHP, Java...), which may query a **database**.
6. The response travels back; the browser renders it.

## Resources you pay for

| Resource | Meaning |
|---|---|
| vCPU | share of processor time |
| RAM | memory for running processes |
| Storage | SSD space (files, database) |
| Bandwidth / egress | data sent out to users |
| Requests / invocations | for serverless |
| Build minutes | for platforms that build your code |

## Domain vs hosting

The **domain** is your address; the **host** is the house. You can buy a domain at one company and host at another, connecting them with DNS records.

## Hosting types at a glance

- **Static hosting** - files only, served from a CDN.
- **Shared hosting** - many sites on one server; cheap, limited.
- **VPS** - your own virtual machine with root access.
- **Dedicated** - a whole physical server.
- **Cloud (IaaS)** - on-demand VMs and services (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud).
- **PaaS** - push code, platform runs it (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku).
- **Serverless** - functions that run per request, billed per use.

The rest of this course explores each one so you can choose wisely.

quiz.q: What is a server?
options: A computer that is always on and serves content over the network
quiz.explain: Servers stay online to answer requests.

quiz.q: Can your domain and hosting be from different companies?
quiz.explain: DNS points the domain at any host.

quiz.q: What is "bandwidth" or "egress" on a hosting bill?
options: The amount of data sent out to visitors
quiz.explain: Egress is outbound data transfer.

lessons.task: Pick three websites you like and use an online "what is my site hosted on" tool or `nslookup` plus an IP lookup to guess where each is hosted. Note whether it seems to use a CDN.

lessons.title: Shared, VPS and dedicated hosting
lessons.summary: Compare classic hosting types by price, control and responsibility.

slides.title: Shared hosting
slides.text:
Many websites on **one** server, sharing CPU and RAM.

- Cheap: a few dollars/month
- Control panel (cPanel, Plesk), one-click WordPress
- PHP + MySQL usually
- Limits: "noisy neighbors", no root access
slides.narration: Shared hosting puts hundreds of websites on one server. It is very cheap and comes with a control panel and one click installers for WordPress. But you share resources with your neighbors, so a busy site next door can slow you down, and you cannot install your own software.

slides.title: VPS
slides.text:
**Virtual Private Server**: your own virtual machine.

- Root access: install anything
- Guaranteed RAM/CPU share
- From ~$4-6/month (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Linode/Akamai, Vultr, AWS Lightsail)
- **You** handle updates, security, backups
slides.narration: A virtual private server gives you your own virtual machine on a shared physical computer. You get root access and can install anything. Small ones cost only a few dollars a month. The catch is that you are now the system administrator, responsible for updates, security and backups.

slides.title: Dedicated server
slides.text:
A whole **physical machine** just for you.

- Maximum performance, no neighbors
- Predictable cost for heavy workloads
- Hardware failures are slower to fix
- From ~$40-100+/month
slides.narration: A dedicated server is a whole physical machine rented just for you. You get all its power with no neighbors, which is great for heavy and steady workloads. But scaling up means renting another machine, and a hardware failure takes longer to fix.

slides.title: First steps on a VPS
slides.text: Basic setup:
slides.narration: When you get a fresh Linux VPS, a few steps come first. Log in with an SSH key, update all packages, create a normal user with sudo rights, and turn on a firewall that only allows SSH and web traffic.
slides.code:
ssh root@203.0.113.10
apt update && apt upgrade -y
adduser deploy && usermod -aG sudo deploy
ufw allow OpenSSH
ufw allow 80,443/tcp
ufw enable
# then: disable password login in /etc/ssh/sshd_config

slides.title: Comparison
slides.text:
| | Shared | VPS | Dedicated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $ | $$ | $$$ |
| Control | low | high | full |
| Your work | little | a lot | a lot |
| Good for | blogs | apps, learning | heavy load |
slides.narration: To compare: shared hosting is cheapest and easiest but limited. A VPS gives lots of control for a small price, and it is a fantastic way to learn. Dedicated servers give full power for heavy loads. In every step up, you take on more responsibility.

lessons.notes:
## Shared hosting

Hundreds of sites share one server's CPU, RAM and disk. The provider manages the operating system, web server (Apache/LiteSpeed/Nginx), PHP and MySQL/MariaDB. You manage files through a control panel (cPanel, Plesk, DirectAdmin) and FTP/SFTP.

- **Pros**: cheap, simple, email often included, good for WordPress or small PHP sites.
- **Cons**: limited resources, noisy neighbors, no root, often only PHP; long-running Node/Python apps may be unsupported.

## VPS (Virtual Private Server)

A hypervisor (KVM, etc.) slices a physical server into virtual machines. You get a full OS (usually Ubuntu or Debian), root access and dedicated RAM.

```bash
ssh deploy@203.0.113.10
sudo apt install nginx
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
```

You are responsible for:
- OS and security updates (`unattended-upgrades` helps),
- firewall (`ufw`), SSH keys only, fail2ban,
- web server, TLS (Certbot or Caddy),
- process manager (systemd, PM2) or Docker,
- **backups** and monitoring.

Providers: Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Akamai (Linode), Vultr, OVHcloud, AWS Lightsail.

## Dedicated servers

A physical machine rented whole. Best for steady, heavy workloads, special hardware (GPUs, lots of disk), or strict isolation. Often cheaper per unit of power than cloud VMs, but less elastic. **Bare-metal cloud** offerings let you order them by API.

## Managed vs unmanaged

"Managed" plans add admin work by the provider (patching, monitoring, support) for extra cost. Unmanaged VPS is cheapest but everything is on you.

## Choosing

- Small WordPress site -> shared or managed WordPress.
- Learning Linux, small apps, side projects -> VPS.
- Big, predictable load -> dedicated or reserved cloud instances.

quiz.q: What is the main downside of shared hosting?
options: Limited resources and control, affected by other sites
quiz.explain: You share resources and lack root access.

quiz.q: What do you get with a VPS that shared hosting lacks?
options: Root access to your own virtual machine
quiz.explain: A VPS gives you full control of a VM.

quiz.q: On an unmanaged VPS, who installs security updates?
quiz.explain: Unmanaged means the server administration is your job.

lessons.task: Compare the cheapest plan of one shared host and one VPS provider: price per month, RAM, CPU, storage, bandwidth, and what you must manage yourself. Decide which you would choose for (a) a family blog and (b) a Node.js API, and explain.

lessons.title: Cloud, PaaS and serverless
lessons.summary: Understand IaaS, PaaS and serverless functions, and pay-as-you-go hosting.

slides.title: The cloud
slides.text:
Rent computing **on demand** by API:
- **AWS**, **Microsoft Azure**, **Google Cloud**
- Plus Oracle, IBM, Alibaba, and smaller clouds

Start a server in seconds, pay per second or hour.
slides.narration: The cloud lets you rent computing on demand. With a few clicks or an API call, you can start a server in seconds and pay only for the time it runs. The big three providers are Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud.

slides.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
slides.text:
- **IaaS**: you get VMs, networks, disks (EC2, Compute Engine)
- **PaaS**: you give code, it runs it (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku, App Engine, Azure App Service)
- **SaaS**: finished software (Gmail, Notion)
slides.narration: Cloud services come in layers. Infrastructure as a service gives you raw virtual machines and networks. Platform as a service takes your code and runs it, handling servers for you. Software as a service is finished software you simply use, like Gmail.

slides.title: Serverless functions
slides.text: Write a function; the platform runs it **per request**.
slides.narration: Serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means you never see them. You write a function, and the platform runs it whenever a request arrives, scaling from zero to thousands of copies. You pay only for the time your code actually runs.

slides.title: Serverless pros and cons
slides.text:
**Pros**: no servers to manage, scales to zero, pay per use

**Cons**: cold starts, time and memory limits, vendor lock-in, costs can jump at high traffic
slides.narration: Serverless is great because there is nothing to manage and it costs nothing when idle. But the first request after a pause can be slow, which is called a cold start. Functions have time limits, your code becomes tied to the provider, and at very high traffic it can cost more than a server.

slides.title: Edge and containers
slides.text:
- **Edge functions**: run in hundreds of locations near users (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel/Netlify Edge, Deno Deploy)
- **Serverless containers**: run any Docker image, scale to zero (Google Cloud Run, AWS App Runner, Azure Container Apps)
slides.narration: Two more options are worth knowing. Edge functions run your code in many cities close to your users, making responses very fast. Serverless containers let you run any Docker image with the same scale to zero billing, giving you more freedom than plain functions.

slides.title: Watch the bill
slides.text:
- Set **budgets and alerts** on day one
- Biggest surprises: data egress, forgotten resources, NAT gateways, logs
- Use free tiers to learn, but read the limits
slides.narration: Pay as you go is flexible, but bills can surprise you. Set a budget alert on the very first day. Common surprises are data transfer out, resources you forgot to delete, and large log volumes. Free tiers are great for learning, just read the limits carefully.

lessons.notes:
## Cloud computing

The **cloud** is on-demand, self-service, pay-as-you-go infrastructure, provisioned by API. Leaders: **AWS**, **Microsoft Azure**, **Google Cloud**; also Oracle Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, IBM, plus developer clouds like DigitalOcean, Hetzner Cloud and Akamai.

## Service models

| Model | You manage | Provider manages | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| IaaS | OS, runtime, app, data | hardware, network, virtualization | AWS EC2, Google Compute Engine, Azure VMs |
| PaaS | app and data | everything below | Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku, Google App Engine, Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk |
| FaaS / serverless | function code | everything else, including scaling | AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Run functions, Azure Functions, Vercel/Netlify Functions, Cloudflare Workers |
| SaaS | your settings | the whole product | Gmail, Shopify |

## Serverless

Functions run in response to events (HTTP requests, queue messages, cron). Billing is per request and per unit of compute time (e.g. GB-seconds).

- **Pros**: zero server maintenance, automatic scaling, scale to zero, often generous free tiers.
- **Cons**: **cold starts** (first request after idle is slower), execution time limits, limited local disk, harder debugging, provider-specific APIs, and per-request costs that can exceed a server at steady high traffic.
- Databases need care: many short-lived functions can open too many connections; use poolers or HTTP-based database drivers.

## Serverless containers

**Google Cloud Run**, **AWS App Runner/ECS Fargate**, **Azure Container Apps**: deploy any container image; billed by use, can scale to zero. A great middle ground.

## Edge computing

Code runs in hundreds of points of presence near users: **Cloudflare Workers**, **Vercel** and **Netlify** edge functions, **Deno Deploy**. Very low latency, but the runtime is restricted (Web APIs, not full Node).

## Cost safety

- Create **budget alerts** immediately.
- Tag resources and delete unused ones.
- Understand **egress** pricing (data leaving the cloud).
- Prefer managed services over hand-built ones when you are small.

quiz.q: Which model gives you raw virtual machines to manage?
quiz.explain: IaaS = infrastructure: VMs, disks, networks.

quiz.q: What is a cold start?
options: A server in a cold data center
Extra delay when a serverless function runs after being idle
quiz.explain: The platform must start a new instance before handling the request.

quiz.q: What should you set up on day one with a cloud account?
quiz.explain: Budget alerts protect you from surprise bills.

lessons.task: Choose one cloud provider and read its free tier page. List three services that are free (with limits) and one service that could unexpectedly cost money. Then create (or plan) a budget alert of $5.

lessons.title: Static hosting: GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages
lessons.summary: Publish static sites for free with modern Git-connected hosts.

slides.title: Static hosting
slides.text:
Upload HTML, CSS, JS, images -> served from a global **CDN**.

- Free for most personal projects
- Automatic HTTPS
- Deploy on `git push`
slides.narration: Static hosts serve plain files from a global content delivery network. For personal projects they are usually free, they add HTTPS automatically, and they redeploy whenever you push to Git. This is the easiest way to get a site online.

slides.title: GitHub Pages
slides.text:
- Free for public repos
- Serve from a branch/folder or build with **GitHub Actions**
- URL: `username.github.io/repo`
- Custom domain + HTTPS
- No server-side code; site size limit ~1 GB
slides.narration: GitHub Pages hosts static sites straight from a GitHub repository. You can serve a folder from a branch, or build your site with GitHub Actions. It is free for public repositories, supports custom domains, and is perfect for portfolios and documentation.

slides.title: Netlify and Vercel
slides.text:
- Connect a repo; framework auto-detected
- **Preview deploys** for every pull request
- Serverless/edge functions for small backend tasks
- Forms, redirects, image optimization
- Vercel is made by the Next.js team
slides.narration: Netlify and Vercel connect to your repository and detect your framework automatically. Every pull request gets its own preview link. Both also offer serverless functions, so you can add small backend features. Vercel is built by the creators of Next.js.

slides.title: Cloudflare Pages / Workers
slides.text:
- Runs on Cloudflare's huge network
- Very generous free bandwidth
- Cloudflare now recommends **Workers with static assets** for new projects (same idea, more features)
- Pairs with Cloudflare DNS
slides.narration: Cloudflare Pages serves sites from Cloudflare's enormous network with very generous free bandwidth. For new projects Cloudflare now recommends Workers with static assets, which works the same way but adds more server features. It fits nicely if your DNS is already on Cloudflare.

slides.title: Deploy in minutes
slides.text: Typical setup:
slides.narration: A typical setup takes minutes. Push your site to GitHub, import the repository on the host, set the build command and output folder, and deploy. You get a free subdomain right away, and you can add your own domain later.
slides.code:
# Vite / React example
Build command:   npm run build
Output folder:   dist
Node version:    24

# plain HTML site
Build command:   (none)
Output folder:   .

slides.title: Read the limits
slides.text:
- **Vercel Hobby**: personal, non-commercial use
- **Netlify** free plan uses monthly credits
- **GitHub Pages**: not for commercial SaaS; soft bandwidth limit
- Plans change: always check the current pricing page
slides.narration: Free plans have rules. Vercel's free Hobby plan is for personal, non-commercial projects. Netlify's free plan uses a monthly credit allowance. GitHub Pages is not meant to run a commercial business. These rules change, so always check the current pricing page.

lessons.notes:
## Why static hosting?

Static sites are files. Hosts copy them to a **CDN** with servers worldwide, so pages load fast everywhere, with nothing to patch or scale.

## The big four

| Host | Highlights | Free plan notes |
|---|---|---|
| **GitHub Pages** | from a repo branch or GitHub Actions; Jekyll support | public repos (private needs paid plan); ~1 GB site, ~100 GB/month soft bandwidth; not for commercial SaaS |
| **Netlify** | previews, forms, functions, redirects (`_redirects`) | credit-based free plan with monthly limits |
| **Vercel** | best-in-class Next.js support, previews, functions, image optimization | Hobby plan is personal, non-commercial |
| **Cloudflare Pages / Workers static assets** | huge network, generous bandwidth, Workers for server code | generous limits on builds and requests |

Others: Render static sites, GitLab Pages, Firebase Hosting, Azure Static Web Apps, AWS Amplify, and object storage (S3, R2) + CDN.

## Typical workflow

1. Push the project to GitHub.
2. Import the repo in the host.
3. Set **build command** (`npm run build`) and **output directory** (`dist`, `build`, `out`, `_site`).
4. Deploy; you get `yourproject.netlify.app` / `.vercel.app` / `.pages.dev`.
5. Add a **custom domain** and DNS records; HTTPS is automatic.

## Single-page apps

React/Vue SPAs need all unknown paths to serve `index.html`. Configure a rewrite, e.g. Netlify `_redirects`:

```
/*  /index.html  200
```

## GitHub Pages with Actions

```yaml
on: { push: { branches: [main] } }
permissions: { pages: write, id-token: write, contents: read }
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: github-pages
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with: { path: . }
      - uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

Always read the host's current pricing and acceptable-use pages: free tiers change often.

quiz.q: What does a static host typically NOT run?
quiz.explain: Static hosts serve files; backend logic needs functions or another host.

quiz.q: Which free plan is limited to personal, non-commercial use?
quiz.explain: Vercel's Hobby plan terms restrict commercial use.

quiz.q: Why does a React SPA need a rewrite rule to index.html?
options: So deep links like /about load the app instead of a 404
quiz.explain: Client-side routes do not exist as files on the server.

lessons.task: Publish a one-page site (an `index.html` with your name and a photo) on **two** different static hosts from the same GitHub repo. Compare how long each took, the URL you got, and the build settings you needed.

lessons.title: Hosting a backend
lessons.summary: Run an API or server-side app in production with a PaaS, container or VPS.

slides.title: What a backend needs
slides.text:
- A **long-running process** listening on a port
- Environment variables and secrets
- A database
- HTTPS in front
- Logs, restarts, health checks
slides.narration: A backend, such as an API in Node, Python or Java, needs more than files. It needs a process that keeps running and listens on a port, configuration and secrets, usually a database, HTTPS in front, and a way to restart it if it crashes.

slides.title: Listen on $PORT
slides.text: Platforms tell your app which port to use:
slides.narration: Most platforms tell your app which port to listen on through an environment variable called PORT. Your code should read it, and listen on all network interfaces, not only localhost, or the platform will not be able to reach it.

slides.title: Option 1: PaaS
slides.text:
**Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku, Koyeb, DigitalOcean App Platform**

- Connect repo or push a Docker image
- Set start command and env vars
- HTTPS, logs, deploys, rollbacks built in
slides.narration: The easiest option is a platform as a service such as Render, Railway, Fly.io or Heroku. Connect your repository or a Docker image, set the start command and environment variables, and the platform handles HTTPS, logs and deploys.

slides.title: Option 2: containers
slides.text:
Build a Docker image, run it on:
- Google Cloud Run, AWS App Runner/ECS, Azure Container Apps
- Any VPS with Docker Compose
- Kubernetes when you grow
slides.narration: Packaging your backend as a Docker image gives you freedom. The same image can run on Google Cloud Run, AWS, Azure, a cheap VPS with Docker Compose, or Kubernetes later. You avoid being locked to one platform.

slides.title: Option 3: your own VPS
slides.text:
Classic stack:

`Internet -> Nginx/Caddy (HTTPS) -> app on 127.0.0.1:3000`

- **systemd** or PM2 keeps the app running
- Nginx/Caddy = **reverse proxy**
slides.narration: On your own server, the classic setup puts a reverse proxy like Nginx or Caddy in front. It handles HTTPS and forwards requests to your app running on a local port. A process manager like systemd keeps the app alive and restarts it after crashes or reboots.

slides.title: Production checklist
slides.text:
- Health endpoint (`/healthz`)
- Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM
- Logs to stdout
- CORS set correctly for your front end
- Rate limiting, input validation
- More than one instance for high availability
slides.narration: Before calling it production ready, add a health endpoint, handle shutdown gracefully, log to standard output, set CORS rules for your front end, and validate inputs. For important services, run at least two instances, so one can fail without downtime.

lessons.notes:
## Requirements of a backend

A backend is a **process** that must keep running, listen on a port, connect to a database, read secrets, and be restarted if it crashes. Hosting it means providing all that.

## Twelve-factor habits

- Read config from env vars (`PORT`, `DATABASE_URL`).
- Bind to `0.0.0.0`, not only `localhost`, inside containers/platforms.
- Log to stdout.
- Be **stateless**: keep sessions and uploads in a database, Redis or object storage (S3, R2), not on local disk, because instances can be replaced at any time.

## Options

| Option | Effort | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| PaaS | lowest | Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku, Koyeb, DigitalOcean App Platform |
| Serverless containers | low | Google Cloud Run, AWS App Runner, Azure Container Apps |
| Functions | low (for small APIs) | AWS Lambda, Vercel/Netlify Functions, Cloudflare Workers |
| VPS | high | Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Linode, Lightsail |
| Kubernetes | highest | EKS, GKE, AKS |

## VPS setup sketch

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/api.service
[Unit]
Description=My API
After=network.target
[Service]
User=deploy
WorkingDirectory=/srv/api
EnvironmentFile=/srv/api/.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js
Restart=always
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```
# Caddyfile - automatic HTTPS
api.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

## Before going live

- Health checks, graceful shutdown.
- CORS limited to your front-end origin.
- Validate input, rate-limit public endpoints.
- Secrets in the platform's secret store.
- Error tracking (Sentry) and uptime monitoring.
- At least two instances for important services.

Many PaaS free tiers sleep idle services (slow first request); paid starter plans keep them always on.

quiz.q: Why should an app read `process.env.PORT`?
options: Because platforms assign the port through that variable
quiz.explain: Platforms set PORT and route traffic to it.

quiz.q: What does a reverse proxy like Nginx or Caddy do in front of your app?
options: Handles HTTPS and forwards requests to the app
quiz.explain: It terminates TLS and passes traffic to the app port.

quiz.q: Why should backend instances be stateless?
options: Because instances can be replaced or scaled, losing local files and memory
quiz.explain: Store state in shared services so any instance can serve any request.

lessons.task: Take a tiny "hello" API (Node, Python or Java) and deploy it to a free or trial PaaS (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Koyeb...). Make it read `PORT` from the environment, add a `/healthz` route, and visit the public URL. Write down every setting you had to configure.

lessons.title: Hosting databases
lessons.summary: Choose between managed databases and running your own, and keep data safe.

slides.title: Where does the data live?
slides.text:
Your app is replaceable. Your **data is not**.

- Relational: **PostgreSQL**, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite
- Document: MongoDB
- Key-value / cache: Redis, Valkey
- Files: object storage (S3, R2)
slides.narration: Your application code can always be redeployed, but your data cannot be recreated. Choosing where it lives is important. Most apps use a relational database like PostgreSQL or MySQL, sometimes with a cache like Redis and object storage for files.

slides.title: Managed databases
slides.text:
The provider runs the server for you:
- Backups, updates, failover
- Examples: AWS RDS/Aurora, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database, **Neon**, **Supabase**, PlanetScale, MongoDB Atlas, Render/Railway Postgres
- Costs more, saves lots of time
slides.narration: A managed database is run for you by a provider. They handle backups, updates and failover. Popular choices include Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL, Neon and Supabase for Postgres, and MongoDB Atlas. It costs more than doing it yourself, but saves a lot of time and risk.

slides.title: Self-hosted
slides.text:
Run Postgres yourself on a VPS or in Docker:
- Cheapest
- **You** must handle backups, upgrades, security, monitoring
- Never expose port 5432/3306 to the internet
slides.narration: You can also run the database yourself on a VPS or in a container. It is the cheapest option, but now backups, upgrades and security are your job. Never expose the database port directly to the internet; only your app should reach it.

slides.title: Connecting safely
slides.text: Connection string in an env var:
slides.narration: Your app connects using a connection string stored in an environment variable. Require TLS for connections that cross the internet. Use a database user with only the permissions the app needs, and use connection pooling, especially with serverless functions.

slides.title: Backups you can trust
slides.text:
- Automatic daily backups + **point-in-time recovery**
- Keep a copy in another region/provider
- **Test restores** regularly
- A backup you never restored is only a hope
slides.narration: Backups matter most. Use automatic daily backups and point in time recovery, keep a copy in a different region, and regularly test that you can restore. A backup you have never restored is only a hope, not a plan.

lessons.notes:
## Kinds of databases

| Type | Examples | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Relational (SQL) | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server | most apps: users, orders |
| Document | MongoDB, Firestore | flexible JSON data |
| Key-value / cache | Redis, Valkey, Memcached | sessions, caching, queues |
| Object storage | AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 | images, uploads, backups |

PostgreSQL is the most popular default for new projects in 2026.

## Managed vs self-hosted

**Managed** (DBaaS): AWS RDS/Aurora, Google Cloud SQL/AlloyDB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL, Neon, Supabase, PlanetScale, Turso (SQLite), MongoDB Atlas, plus databases built into Render, Railway, Fly.io and DigitalOcean.

- Automated backups, patches, high availability, metrics.
- Scale with a click; some offer **serverless** Postgres that scales to zero and **branching** for previews.

**Self-hosted**: Postgres on your VPS or in Docker. Cheapest, full control, but you own backups, upgrades, replication and security.

## Connection basics

- Store the connection string in `DATABASE_URL`.
- Require TLS (`sslmode=require`) over public networks.
- Use **least-privilege** users; never let the app connect as the superuser.
- Keep the database on a private network or allow-list app IPs. Never expose 5432/3306 publicly with weak passwords.
- Use a **connection pooler** (PgBouncer, built-in poolers) with serverless functions.

## Migrations

Change schemas with versioned migration tools (Prisma Migrate, Drizzle, Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, Django migrations), run automatically in CI/CD, and keep them backward compatible.

## Backups

- Daily snapshots + **point-in-time recovery (PITR)**.
- Off-site copy (another region or provider).
- Encryption at rest.
- **Test restores** on a schedule.

```bash
pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" -Fc -f backup.dump
pg_restore -d "$TEST_DATABASE_URL" backup.dump
```

quiz.q: What is a main benefit of a managed database?
options: The provider handles backups, patches and failover
quiz.explain: Managed services take over operational work.

quiz.q: Which practice is UNSAFE?
options: Exposing the database port publicly with the superuser account
quiz.explain: Public databases with powerful users are a common breach cause.

quiz.q: Why test restoring backups?
options: Because a backup is only proven useful once you have restored it successfully
quiz.explain: Untested backups often fail when you need them.

lessons.task: Plan the data layer for a small online shop: which database (managed or self-hosted, which provider), where product images go, how backups work (frequency, retention, location), and the steps you would take to test a restore.

lessons.title: CDNs: content delivery networks
lessons.summary: Make sites fast worldwide by caching content close to users.

slides.title: Distance is slow
slides.text:
Light in fiber is fast, but not instant.

Server in Frankfurt, user in Sydney: ~250+ ms per round trip.

A page needs many round trips.
slides.narration: Even at the speed of light, distance matters. If your server is in Europe and your visitor is in Australia, each round trip takes a quarter of a second or more, and a page needs many round trips. That makes the site feel slow.

slides.title: What a CDN does
slides.text:
A **CDN** has servers (**PoPs**) in hundreds of cities.

- Caches your files near users
- First request -> fetched from your **origin**
- Next requests -> served from the nearby cache
slides.narration: A content delivery network has servers in hundreds of cities, called points of presence. The first time a file is requested in a region, the CDN fetches it from your origin server and keeps a copy. Everyone nearby then gets it from that local copy, which is much faster.

slides.title: Cache-Control
slides.text: You control caching with HTTP headers:
slides.narration: You tell the CDN and browsers how long to cache with the Cache Control header. Files with a hash in their name can be cached for a year, because a new version gets a new name. HTML usually gets a short cache or must be revalidated.
slides.code:
# fingerprinted assets: app.3f9a2c.js
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# HTML pages
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate

# private user data
Cache-Control: private, no-store

slides.title: More than caching
slides.text:
- **DDoS protection** and a web application firewall (WAF)
- Free TLS, HTTP/3
- Image optimization, compression (Brotli)
- Edge functions
- Hides your origin IP
slides.narration: Modern CDNs do much more than cache. They absorb denial of service attacks, filter malicious requests with a firewall, handle TLS and HTTP three, compress and resize images, and can even run code at the edge.

slides.title: Providers
slides.text:
- **Cloudflare** (generous free plan)
- Fastly, Akamai
- AWS CloudFront, Google Cloud CDN, Azure Front Door
- Bunny.net
- Built in: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages
slides.narration: Popular CDNs include Cloudflare, which has a generous free plan, Fastly, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront and Bunny dot net. Static hosts like Vercel and Netlify already include a CDN, so you get one automatically.

lessons.notes:
## Why CDNs

Latency is dominated by distance and the number of round trips (DNS, TCP/QUIC, TLS, HTTP). A **CDN** places caches in hundreds of **points of presence (PoPs)** so most requests are answered nearby, reducing latency and load on your **origin** server.

## How caching works

1. User in Tokyo requests `/app.3f9a2c.js`.
2. Tokyo PoP has no copy (**cache miss**) -> fetches from origin, stores it.
3. Next Tokyo users get a **cache hit**: fast, origin untouched.

Your **cache hit ratio** (hits / total) is a key metric; aim high.

## Controlling caches

```
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable   # hashed assets
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300
Cache-Control: private, no-store                      # personal data
```

- **Fingerprint** filenames (`app.3f9a2c.js`) so you can cache forever; bundlers do this automatically.
- **Purge** (invalidate) cached files after deploys when needed.
- `s-maxage` sets a different TTL for shared caches like CDNs.
- Never cache responses containing personal data publicly.

## Extra features

- TLS termination, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC).
- Brotli/gzip compression, image resizing and modern formats (AVIF/WebP).
- **DDoS mitigation**, **WAF**, bot management, rate limiting.
- Edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, CloudFront Functions).
- Origin shielding: one PoP fetches from origin for the others.

## Providers

Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront, Google Cloud CDN, Azure Front Door, Bunny.net. Static hosts (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages) include a CDN.

## Using a CDN with your own server

Point DNS at the CDN (or enable a proxy like Cloudflare's orange cloud), set origin to your server, configure caching rules, and lock the origin firewall so only the CDN can reach it.

quiz.q: What is the "origin" in CDN terms?
options: Your actual server where the original content lives
quiz.explain: The CDN fetches from the origin on a cache miss.

quiz.q: Why can `app.3f9a2c.js` be cached for a year?
options: A new version gets a new file name (hash), so old caches never serve wrong code
quiz.explain: Fingerprinting makes long caching safe.

quiz.q: Which content should NOT be publicly cached?
quiz.explain: Personal data must use private or no-store.

lessons.task: Open your browser developer tools (Network tab) on a big website. Pick three files (an image, a JS file, the HTML page) and record their `Cache-Control` header and any CDN headers like `cf-cache-status`, `x-cache` or `age`. Explain what each tells you.

lessons.title: Uptime, backups and disaster recovery
lessons.summary: Keep your site available and your data recoverable when things go wrong.

slides.title: What uptime numbers mean
slides.text:
| Uptime | Downtime per year |
|---|---|
| 99% | ~3.65 days |
| 99.9% | ~8.8 hours |
| 99.99% | ~53 minutes |
| 99.999% | ~5 minutes |
slides.narration: Hosts advertise uptime as a percentage. Ninety nine percent sounds great, but it allows more than three days of downtime a year. Ninety nine point nine allows under nine hours, and each extra nine is much harder and more expensive to achieve.

slides.title: SLAs
slides.text:
A **Service Level Agreement** promises uptime.

- If broken, you usually get **service credits**, not your lost revenue
- Read what counts as downtime
- Your app's uptime <= the weakest dependency
slides.narration: A service level agreement is the host's promise of uptime. If they miss it, you usually get a small credit on your bill, not compensation for lost sales. And remember your app can only be as reliable as all the services it depends on combined.

slides.title: Monitor from outside
slides.text:
- External uptime checks every 1-5 minutes (UptimeRobot, Better Stack, Pingdom, Checkly)
- Alerts by email, SMS, chat
- Public **status page** for users
- Also watch certificate and domain expiry
slides.narration: Monitor your site from the outside, the way users see it. Uptime services check your site every minute or so from many locations and alert you when it fails. A public status page keeps users informed, and you should also watch certificate and domain expiry dates.

slides.title: The 3-2-1 backup rule
slides.text:
- **3** copies of your data
- on **2** different types of storage
- **1** off-site (another region/provider)

Plus: one copy that cannot be deleted (immutable) to resist ransomware.
slides.narration: The three two one rule is a classic for backups: keep three copies of your data, on two different types of storage, with one copy off site. Today many add one immutable copy that cannot be deleted, which protects against ransomware and mistakes.

slides.title: RPO and RTO
slides.text:
- **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective): how much data can you afford to lose? (e.g. 1 hour)
- **RTO** (Recovery Time Objective): how long can you be down? (e.g. 4 hours)

They decide how often you back up and how you restore.
slides.narration: Two numbers guide disaster planning. The recovery point objective is how much data you can afford to lose, for example one hour. The recovery time objective is how long you can be offline. These numbers decide how often to back up and how fast your restore must be.

slides.title: Redundancy
slides.text:
- Multiple instances behind a load balancer
- Multiple **availability zones**
- Database replicas with automatic failover
- Infrastructure as code to rebuild quickly
- Practice: restore drills, failover tests
slides.narration: Redundancy removes single points of failure. Run several app instances behind a load balancer, spread across availability zones, and use database replicas with automatic failover. Keep your infrastructure as code so you can rebuild quickly, and practice restores regularly.

lessons.notes:
## Measuring availability

Uptime % over a period. Each extra "nine" cuts allowed downtime by 10x:

| Target | Per month | Per year |
|---|---|---|
| 99% | ~7.3 h | ~3.65 days |
| 99.9% | ~43.8 min | ~8.8 h |
| 99.99% | ~4.4 min | ~53 min |

## SLAs

A provider's **SLA** defines promised uptime and compensation (usually service credits). Your overall availability multiplies: an app depending on three 99.9% services can be down more than any one of them.

## Monitoring

- **External uptime checks** (UptimeRobot, Better Stack, Checkly, Pingdom, Uptime Kuma self-hosted): HTTP checks, keyword checks, SSL expiry, domain expiry.
- **Status page** to communicate incidents.
- Alerts routed to the person on call.

## Backups

The **3-2-1 rule**: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site. Modern additions: **1 immutable** (object lock) copy and **0 errors** after verified restores (3-2-1-1-0).

Back up:
- databases (snapshots + PITR),
- user uploads (object storage with versioning),
- configuration and infrastructure code (in Git),
- secrets (in a secret manager with its own backup).

## RPO and RTO

- **RPO** - maximum acceptable data loss, sets backup frequency.
- **RTO** - maximum acceptable downtime, sets restore method (restore from snapshot vs hot standby).

## Redundancy patterns

- Load balancer + 2+ app instances.
- Spread across **availability zones** (separate data centers in a region).
- Managed database with standby replica and automatic failover.
- Multi-region only when the business truly needs it; it is complex and expensive.
- **Infrastructure as Code** (Terraform/OpenTofu, Pulumi) to recreate environments.

## Practice

Run restore drills and game days. Write a runbook: who does what, in which order, and how to communicate.

quiz.q: About how much downtime per year does 99.9% uptime allow?
quiz.explain: 0.1% of a year is about 8.76 hours.

quiz.q: What does the "1" in the 3-2-1 backup rule stand for?
quiz.explain: At least one copy must be stored in another location.

quiz.q: What does RPO describe?
options: How much data loss you can accept
quiz.explain: Recovery Point Objective = acceptable data loss window.

lessons.task: Create a free uptime check (UptimeRobot, Better Stack or Uptime Kuma) for a site you own or a public test page. Then write a mini disaster recovery plan for your project: RPO, RTO, what is backed up, where, how often, and the restore steps.

lessons.title: Choosing a host and estimating costs
lessons.summary: Compare hosting options for real projects and estimate monthly costs.

slides.title: Start from requirements
slides.text:
- What are you hosting? (static, API, database, files)
- Expected traffic and growth
- Team skills and time
- Budget
- Compliance and location (e.g. GDPR, data in the EU)
slides.narration: Choosing a host starts with requirements, not brand names. What exactly are you hosting? How much traffic do you expect? What skills and time does your team have? What is the budget? And are there legal rules, like keeping data inside the European Union?

slides.title: Common good choices
slides.text:
| Project | Good fit |
|---|---|
| Portfolio, docs, blog | static host (free) |
| WordPress site | managed WordPress / shared |
| Side-project API | PaaS or Cloud Run |
| Learning Linux | small VPS |
| Growing SaaS | PaaS/containers + managed DB |
| Large org | cloud + Kubernetes |
slides.narration: Some patterns work well. A portfolio or blog fits a free static host. A WordPress site fits managed WordPress hosting. A side project API fits a platform as a service. To learn Linux, get a small VPS. A growing company often uses containers with a managed database.

slides.title: Estimating cost
slides.text:
Add up:
- compute (instances x hours)
- database
- storage
- **egress** bandwidth
- extras: backups, logs, monitoring, domains, email

Use each provider's pricing calculator.
slides.narration: To estimate cost, add up compute, database, storage, outbound bandwidth and the extras like backups, logs and monitoring. Do not forget the domain and email. Every big provider has a pricing calculator to help.

slides.title: A sample monthly budget
slides.text:
```
Static front end (free tier)      $0
PaaS API, 1 small instance        $7
Managed Postgres, small           $15-25
Object storage 20 GB              $1
Domain (~$12/yr)                  $1
Uptime + error tracking (free)    $0
--------------------------------------
~ $25-35 / month
```
slides.narration: Here is a realistic small budget. A static front end on a free tier, a small API instance for around seven dollars, a small managed Postgres database for fifteen to twenty five dollars, a little object storage, and the domain. Around thirty dollars a month runs a real product for many users.

slides.title: Avoid lock-in and traps
slides.text:
- Prefer open standards: Docker, Postgres, S3 API
- Watch egress fees and per-seat pricing
- Free tiers can change or sleep
- Check support quality and region locations
- Keep exportable backups
slides.narration: Think about the future. Using open standards like Docker containers, Postgres and the S3 storage API makes it easier to move later. Watch for egress fees, free tiers that change, and support quality. Always keep backups you can take elsewhere.

slides.title: Decide and revisit
slides.text:
1. Pick the **simplest** option that meets needs
2. Set budget alerts
3. Measure real usage
4. Revisit every few months
slides.narration: The professional approach is to start with the simplest option that meets your needs, set budget alerts, measure your real usage, and revisit the decision every few months. You can always move to something more powerful when you truly need it.

lessons.notes:
## Decision questions

1. **What** are you running? Static files, server code, database, background jobs, file uploads?
2. **How much** traffic now and in a year?
3. **Who** maintains it? Do you want to manage servers?
4. **Where** are users and where must data stay (GDPR, data residency)?
5. **Budget** and how predictable it must be.

## Matching needs to hosting

| Need | Suggested |
|---|---|
| Static site | GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare |
| WordPress | managed WordPress or quality shared hosting |
| API / web app (small) | Render, Railway, Fly.io, Koyeb, Google Cloud Run |
| Full control, low cost | VPS (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Linode) |
| Heavy steady load | dedicated / reserved instances |
| Many services, big team | AWS/Azure/GCP with containers or Kubernetes |

## Cost components

- **Compute**: instance size x hours (or requests x duration for serverless).
- **Database**: instance size, storage, backups, replicas.
- **Storage**: GB-month plus request fees.
- **Egress**: data out to the internet (often the surprise; Cloudflare R2 charges no egress).
- **Extras**: load balancers, NAT gateways, logs, monitoring, support plans, email, domains.

Use calculators: AWS Pricing Calculator, Google Cloud Pricing Calculator, Azure Pricing Calculator.

## Saving money

- Right-size: start small, scale on evidence.
- Turn off idle dev/staging resources.
- Use committed-use discounts or reserved instances for steady loads.
- Cache with a CDN to cut origin load and egress.
- Delete old snapshots and logs on a retention schedule.

## Avoiding lock-in

Favor portable building blocks: containers, PostgreSQL/MySQL, S3-compatible storage, OpenTelemetry, Terraform/OpenTofu. Keep backups exportable.

## Revisit

Hosting is not a one-time decision. Review usage and bills every few months and adjust. Moving from a free tier to a paid plan, or from PaaS to containers, is normal growth.

quiz.q: What should drive your hosting choice first?
options: Your requirements: workload, traffic, skills, budget, compliance
quiz.explain: Start from requirements, then match options.

quiz.q: Which cost is often a surprise in the cloud?
quiz.explain: Egress fees can grow quickly with traffic.

quiz.q: How do open standards like Docker, Postgres and the S3 API help?
options: They make it easier to move between providers
They remove the need for backups
quiz.explain: Portable tools reduce vendor lock-in.

lessons.task: Choose a real or imagined project (for example, a school club website with logins and photo uploads). Write a one-page hosting plan: chosen providers for front end, backend, database and files; a monthly cost estimate with a table; how you will back up; and what would make you switch hosts later.
